Issued at 251 PM CDT Sun Sep 13 2026

Weak, quasi-zonal flow continues today with the surface boundary 
having slid to the south of the forecast area. Overnight showers and 
storms had mostly waned by sunrise, though some renewed development 
was observed in eastern Kansas earlier this morning. A cursory 
mesoanalysis investigation yielded the discovery of small area 
of low- level frontogenesis that helped promote this resurgence 
on the edge of a weakening low-level jet. Showers and storms 
continued to work their way into our southeastern Kansas 
counties this afternoon. With cloud tops warming substantially 
over the course of the day, only a couple of light showers 
remain with most remaining dry. 

As we proceed into the late evening and overnight period, our rain 
chances will increase once again as the low-level jet ramps up over 
the Plains and kicks off elevated showers and storms. PWATs are 
forecast to rise to around 1.8" with the moisture surge. With 
elevated instability and shear, there may be a brief period 
overnight where we could see some small hail and gustier winds, but 
even these more organized storms should remain sub-severe. The main 
concern would be heavy rainfall, particularly within a corridor 
south of US-36 and between I-35 and US-65. It is just to the 
northwest of this corridor where development is expected to occur on 
the nose of the intensifying low-level jet roughly around midnight. 
Northwesterly steering flow will guide storms to the southeast along 
a strong 310K isentropic gradient as the night progresses, further 
fueling efficient warm rain processes. WPC has highlighted the 
northwestern and western portions of the forecast area in a Slight 
Risk (Level 2 of 4) of excessive rainfall for reasons such as these. 

Warmer conditions are expected on Monday as a warm front approaches 
from the southwest. The question of how warm it will be depends 
heavily on the speed of the boundary with cloud cover clearing in 
its wake. Currently, maximum temperatures in our far south are 
forecast to top out in the mid 90s, but this is assuming we clear 
out rapidly after sunrise. Dewpoints in the low/mid 70s will keep 
heat index values mostly in the upper 90s but some locations that 
are able to heat up quickly may be able to approach 105. The warm 
front is not expected to make it through northeast Missouri by 
sunset, so temperatures may only top out in the low/mid 80s in those 
areas. 

Behind the warm front and ahead of an approaching cold front, 
isolated storms may be possible across northwestern Missouri late 
Monday afternoon and evening. By this time, moderate instability 
will have built in across the region with around 35-40 kts of deep-
layer shear. There is a non-zero chance of some sort of discrete 
development in the warm sector, but this potential seems to be 
highest further north in eastern Nebraska and southern Iowa. 
Currently, it seems the more likely scenario for far northwest 
Missouri is that it gets clipped by upscale growth along the cold 
front later Monday night. SPC has highlighted a sliver of northwest 
Missouri in a Slight Risk (Level 2 of 5) for severe weather tomorrow 
night for which all hazards could be possible. The severe threat 
would likely peak between 6 PM and 9 PM before gradually lessening 
through the overnight period. 

The cold front will continue moving to the southeast over the course 
of the day on Tuesday, bringing widespread rain and storm chances to 
the region (best chances remain north of I-70 but still have 40-50% 
PoPs further south). Much of the forecast area is encompassed in an 
SPC Marginal Risk (Level 1 of 5) that day, but the greatest threat 
remains the heavy rainfall with PWATs in excess of 2.0" and very 
strong isentropic ascent parallel to the boundary and on the nose of 
the low-level jet. Except for a few of our southeast counties, WPC 
has enshrouded the area in another Slight Risk (Level 2 of 4) of 
excessive rainfall on Tuesday. By Wednesday morning, the cold front 
will have effectively stalled out along our southern CWA border, 
only to ever so slightly drift back northward over the course of the 
day. Though the setup is not quite as concerning from a rainfall 
production standpoint, any additional rain on top of what had fallen 
on Tuesday could exacerbate any existing flooding and flash flooding 
concerns. That is, by Wednesday, it doesn't appear that it will take 
much cause flooding problems, and for this, WPC has included areas 
generally north of I-70 in yet another Slight Risk (Level 2 of 4) 
for excessive rainfall. Additional rainfall is possible Thursday and 
beyond but these forecasts are lower confidence at this stage. 
Regardless, between now and Friday night, we could see a large swath 
of 3"+ total rain accumulations across northwestern Missouri and 
northeastern Kansas, with isolated spots potentially exceeding 5".
